segmentIncome.title: Adjusted operating income by segment
segmentIncome.content:
Prudential reports results across seven segments: PGIM (asset management fees), Retirement Strategies (institutional & individual annuities/pension risk transfer), Group Insurance, Individual Life, International Businesses (chiefly Japan), US Legacy Products (Closed Block/run-off), and Corporate & Other (holding-company interest expense, Divested and Run-off businesses).

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: International has been the segment most disrupted this year — the Prudential of Japan FSA sales suspension (voluntary pause escalated to a formal regulatory order, extended into 2027) has cut new Japan sales, and Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia and Kenya have been reclassified out of International into Divested and Run-off business (inside Corporate & Other) ahead of their sale/exit, so International's YoY comparison understates the surviving Japan-plus-Europe franchise. Corporate & Other is structurally negative (holdco interest, run-off drag) and should not be read as an operating loss.

What to watch:

  • Whether PGIM and Retirement Strategies (the two segments management is growing) keep offsetting the International decline
  • International income once Japan sales resume and the divested units fully exit Corporate & Other
  • Corporate & Other narrowing as divestiture proceeds reduce holdco debt

flows.title: Net flows and third-party flows
flows.content:
Net flows are client money in minus money out across PGIM and the retirement/annuity businesses in a period ($bn); third-party flows are the subset from external (non-general-account) clients, the purer read on PGIM's distribution strength.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: flows drive future fee revenue independently of markets — AUM can rise on market performance even with weak flows, or fall on redemptions even with strong markets. Record retail annuity sales have supported Retirement Strategies flows this year even as International flows soften with the Japan suspension.

What to watch:

  • Net flows turning persistently negative (redemptions outrunning sales)
  • Third-party flows versus total flows — a rising external share means PGIM is winning outside business, not just managing Prudential's own general account

aum.title: Assets under management
aum.content:
AUM is the value of client assets the firm manages or administers.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: fee income scales with AUM; flows and market moves both drive it.

What to watch:

  • Net flows versus market performance

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Prudential Financial, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
